name: Turkey illusion
statement: The turkey illusion is the error of treating a situation of uncertainty as one of calculable risk, so confidence peaks just before the break.
meaning: Gerd Gigerenzer states the target plainly in his 2020 handbook chapter: 'Many psychologists do not distinguish between risk and uncertainty but instead believe that all problems can be solved by probability theory, as assumed in Bayesian theories of mind or brain. This position has been criticized as being the "turkey illusion."' The distinction he draws is Frank Knight's, whose 1921 book the chapter cites. Under risk the outcomes and their probabilities are known, and calculation suffices. Under uncertainty the set of outcomes is not known, and surprises happen. In the parable the turkey updates on the only two outcomes it can imagine, fed or not fed, and by Bayesian updating its confidence is highest on day 100. That day is the one before Thanksgiving. Gigerenzer's own gloss is that the turkey 'missed a crucial piece of information: It was not in a situation of risk, where the past predicts the future.' He applies the charge to institutions rather than to birds, writing that it 'appears to be committed more frequently by humans than turkeys'. The illusion is a criticism of how uncertainty is modelled, not a claim about a measurable tendency in individuals.

origin.note: No source claiming to have coined the phrase was located. The earliest dated use found is the German form, Truthahn-Illusion, in the headline of a May 2013 interview with Gigerenzer by Heike Littger in managerSeminare, issue 182. The interview accompanied his book 'Risiko: Wie man die richtigen Entscheidungen trifft', which the German National Library catalogue records as Munich, Bertelsmann, 2013, 396 pages, translated from the English by Hainer Kober. The English text appeared in 2014 as 'Risk Savvy: How to Make Good Decisions', whose chapter 2 is titled 'Certainty Is an Illusion'. Neither book's text was obtained, so this entry does not claim the phrase appears in either. Gigerenzer uses it in print in the 2020 chapter cited below, where he attributes the story, and not the label, to Russell and Taleb.

evidence: No experiment on the turkey illusion was located. Gigerenzer presents it as the third of three criticisms of choice axioms, alongside a descriptive and a prescriptive objection, and offers no data for it. Its support in the chapter is the worked parable and one historical case. He writes of 'the increasing confidence of financial institutions in the stability of the financial market in the years before the crisis of 2007-2008, up to shortly before the breakdown', and adds that the rating agencies calibrated their models on the past years and predicted that the future resembles the past. No figure, dataset or named agency accompanies that claim. The chapter's other illustration is Taleb's Las Vegas casino, whose main losses came from a tiger attacking the star performer, a disgruntled former contractor's attempt to dynamite the building, and an employee who failed to file tax reports for a long period. Gigerenzer cites Taleb 2007, pages 129 to 130, for it. The measured work the chapter attaches to the risk and uncertainty distinction sits one step away from the illusion, and both descriptions below are the chapter's rather than this entry's reading of the papers. It reports that Ellsberg showed people's preferences over gambles to be sensitive to whether the probabilities are known or ambiguous. It also lists the 1/N rule, allocating resources equally across N alternatives, with the note that it can outperform optimal asset allocation portfolios, citing DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal. Neither of those two papers was read for this entry.

replication.headline: No replication attempt was found, because there is no original study to repeat. The turkey illusion is a name for a way of modelling badly, and nobody appears to have turned it into a claim about people that could pass or fail.
replication.detail: Europe PMC returns no records for 'turkey illusion' or for 'Truthahn-Illusion'. arXiv returns none. Crossref returns no work whose title carries the phrase. Gigerenzer's own chapter cites no study for it and reports no data. The nearest measured relative is ambiguity aversion, and it is a different claim. Ambiguity aversion concerns known against vague probabilities over a fixed set of outcomes, while the turkey illusion concerns a set of outcomes the decision maker never imagined. Counting work on the first as a test of the second would be the error the entry warns about.

limits: The search for a study covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, Europe PMC for both the English and the German phrase, arXiv, and general web search. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and the Google Books API each refused the request for want of quota or rate, so those three indexes went unsearched. Neither 'Risk Savvy' nor 'Risiko' was obtained. The Internet Archive holds a lending-restricted scan of the former and its search-inside endpoints returned errors, and no full text of either book was reachable. This entry therefore cannot say on which page, or in which of the two books, the phrase first reached print, and its 2013 date rests on a magazine headline rather than on the book. Two further items named by the German Wikipedia article were unreachable: Der Spiegel 12/2013 behind a paywall, and a 2014 blog account of a Gigerenzer talk behind an egress block. The 2020 chapter was read in a full-text copy of the handbook's second edition posted at dokumen.pub rather than at Cambridge, and the turkey passage was fetched twice with identical wording. Chalmers was read in the third edition of 1999; earlier editions were not checked.
misreadings: The story is credited to Russell, and Russell wrote about a chicken. Chapter VI of his 'The Problems of Philosophy' of 1912 says that 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.' There is no turkey, no nine o'clock feeding, no Christmas and no named illusion. The turkey arrives with Alan Chalmers, whose 'What Is This Thing Called Science?' gives at page 45 of the third edition 'a somewhat gruesome example attributed to Bertrand Russell' about a bird fed at 9 am whose throat is cut on Christmas eve. Chalmers writes 'attributed to', and the term inductivist turkey appears nowhere in the text of that edition as searched for this entry. The credit hardens anyway. Kováč's 2013 note in EMBO Reports calls it the famous parable of Bertrand Russell's inductivist turkey, the German Wikipedia article cites that note for the claim that Russell described the bias, and the English article repeats the claim. The English article cites Gigerenzer for it, and Gigerenzer says the opposite in the same sentence: the illusion 'goes back to the philosopher Bertrand Russell (who used a chicken in his account), and has been popularized by trader Nassim Taleb'. Taleb is the second stop and is the more careful of the two. His footnote to chapter 4 of 'The Black Swan' reads 'Since Russell's original example used a chicken, this is the enhanced North American adaptation.' The phrase turkey illusion does not occur in the scanned text of that book searched for this entry. The last error is to file the illusion with the cognitive biases and expect an effect size. Gigerenzer aims it at psychologists who model uncertainty as risk, and at rating agencies, not at a tendency measured in individuals.

sources.text: Gigerenzer, G. (2020). Intelligence and Decision-Making. In R. J. Sternberg (Ed.), The Cambridge Handbook of Intelligence, 2nd ed. (pp. 580-601). Cambridge University Press. The section 'The Turkey Illusion' is at page 586. Read as the full text of the second edition posted at dokumen.pub; the passage was fetched twice and matched.

Littger, H. (2013). Gerd Gigerenzer über Risikointelligenz: 'Die Truthahn-Illusion leitet uns fehl'. managerSeminare, issue 182, May 2013. The headline, author, issue and date were read at the publisher's article page, fetched twice.

Deutsche Nationalbibliothek catalogue record for Gigerenzer, G. (2013). Risiko: Wie man die richtigen Entscheidungen trifft. Munich: Bertelsmann, 396 pages, ISBN 978-3-570-10103-2, 'Aus dem Engl. von Hainer Kober'. Source for the German edition's publisher, year and translation.

Table of contents of Gigerenzer, G., Risk Savvy: How to Make Good Decisions, Penguin Books edition, ISBN 978-0-241-95461-4, scanned by the ETH Zurich library. Source for the chapter titles and page ranges quoted here, including chapter 2, 'Certainty Is an Illusion', pages 17 to 42. The body text of the book was not obtained.
Russell, B. (1912). The Problems of Philosophy. Chapter VI, 'On Induction', supplies the chicken passage. Read as the Project Gutenberg plain text, ebook 5827.

Chalmers, A. F. (1999). What Is This Thing Called Science? Third edition, Hackett Publishing Company, reprinted from the University of Queensland Press third edition. The turkey passage is at page 45, in chapter 4, 'Deriving theories from the facts: induction'. Read as a scanned PDF with a text layer.

Taleb, N. N. (2007). The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable. Chapter 4, 'One Thousand and One Days, or How Not to Be a Sucker', and its endnote on Russell's chicken. Read as the scanned full text at the Internet Archive.
Kováč, L. (2013). Homo artefaciens. EMBO Reports, 14(6), 482. Full text read at Europe PMC, PMC3674451. The source the German Wikipedia article cites for attributing the parable to Russell.
Wikipedia, 'Truthahn-Illusion' and 'Turkey illusion', wikitext read on 9 August 2026. Cited as the object of the attribution error described above, not as evidence for anything.

Ellsberg, D. (1961). Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 75(4), 643-669. Cited by Gigerenzer's chapter for the ambiguity result described above. Not obtained for this entry.

DeMiguel, V., Garlappi, L., & Uppal, R. (2009). Optimal versus naive diversification: How inefficient is the 1/N portfolio strategy? Review of Financial Studies, 22(5), 1915-1953. Cited by Gigerenzer's chapter for the 1/N rule. Not obtained for this entry.
